plan.english: Worm, go out of the bone, go out of the blood! Do not devour the blood, do not suck the sore. The worm is dead, and the sore is gone. Let it grow strong, and let the dear blood be in it. May the god protect you, and may Dawn guard you.

The god went out, the horse's bone broke. Three times he spoke the dear word. Mother Earth, join bone with bone! Join dear blood with blood! The bone grew strong, and the blood was joined. May this man's dear bone grow strong.

Blood, stand still, and do not go out! I lay a cord around the sore. May the eye of the sun look upon it. May the sun dry the blood. The door is shut, the blood stays within. Thrice I speak the word to you.

What burns in the dear heart, let that grow cold! Water, come to the man and to his bones! Now let him lie down and sweat. May the dear fire go away. Night shall carry it away. Dawn shines, and he lives.

Swift snake, creeping in the furrow, lie down! Do not go to the sheep or the shepherd. Now the dog is awake, he sees you. Creep away, now go down to the bottom. May no one be lost, man and beast alike.

title: Keep the wolf from the sheep

plan.english: Wolf, do not seize the shepherd's dear sheep! The shepherd and the dog protect them. And now go away to the wild beasts. Perkunos, guard the sheep, and let the wolf flee from the dear door and the field. The dog is awake, and let the wolf not come.

Night has come, and the master has lain down. Thief, do not come to the master's dear door! Let your eyes not see. Now, thief, let your arm go slack. The dog is awake, and the god guards the home. Whoever steals the cattle, let him die.

title: Do not tremble in the night

plan.english: Son, do not tremble in the night! Your mother is near. The good god is near. He protects you, and the good dog is awake. May a good dream come to you. And now night flees, and it dawns again.

Father Dyeus, let it rain on the grain! Mother Earth, bear it. Yoke the cattle, and let us plough the furrow. May the grain increase in the furrow. May the good sun ripen it. May the sheep be fat. May the work succeed, and may the yoke not break.

Now, cattle, come home to your own village! The shepherd leads you. Now the man follows along. It is getting dark. Do not slip away, let no one be lost. At the door the mistress milks the cattle. In the dwelling the bright blaze burns.

Now, Father Dyeus, may it rain, may it rain! Perkunos, strike the oak. Now the water comes down from the sky. The earth is thirsty; let her drink and be full. Then the grain will grow, great is this gift.

Much fire, burn the grubs in the wool! Burn the worms, burn the eggs. Do not burn the wool, do not burn the dwelling. Be bright, wool of the sheep. And now the man smears it with honey. The grubs shall die in it.

I lay a cord around your heart. Let your heart come forward to me, let your mind follow me. And now the oak stands by its root. And now let your love stand firm by the cord, and may the cord not break in the night.

Perkunos has seen the hearts of men. Whoever deceives the guest, let him vanish. Let the oath stand; it is great. He who guards the pledge shall live. The gods have heard the word of the oath. Lead the guest into the dwelling.

The wife went to the healer and said: 'My husband lies down, and the sore on his arm is red.' He said: 'What did he eat? What did he drink?' She said: 'He ate nothing; he drank water.' 'Smear it with honey, and cover it with wool. When the sun shines, it will dry.'

A wolf came to the sheep. The shepherd stood and drove it away, but the beast wounded him. His arm was red with blood. His wife saw him and cried out. She seized wool, covered the arm, and smeared it with honey. Three nights he lay in the home. Then he stood up. The beast did not come again.

When someone's bone breaks, straighten the arm. Cover it with wool and lay a cord around it. Give him mead, and let him drink. Let him not stand up, but let him lie down. When nine nights have gone, let him rise. If the bone does not grow strong, do not be afraid: seek the one who knows.

title: The mother sits by her son

plan.english: The son's heart burned. His mother sat beside him and carried water. She said: 'Dyeus, hear me! Heal my son! Give him strength!' Then he sweated, and the fire vanished from him. At dawn he saw her and spoke: 'Mother, I am thirsty.' She gave him mead.

Dawn, bright goddess, hear us, you who split the night, you who lead the sun! Give light to the eyes of this man, and heal his sore. May the wheel of the sun carry the sorrow away. Dry the blood, and let him wake up. May he live and see your light again.
The horse lay in the field and did not eat. The man saw it: the bone was broken. He straightened the bone and covered it. He brought grain and gave it to the horse. Then the horse stood and ate.

The ox stood trembling at the door. In its sore were worms, and they were devouring the blood. The wife heated water, and it boiled. The shepherd seized the worms and threw them into the fire. Then he smeared it with honey. Then the ox ate, and it was not afraid.

The king lay down, and the healer sat beside him. 'Shall I live?' 'King, you shall live, if you lie down and drink.' 'What shall I give you?' 'Give me nothing. Give Dyeus a gift.' Then the king gave him a gift, and awoke.

title: The law of the wounded man

plan.english: If a man wounds a man, let him heal him and give him a reward. If the man dies, let him give a hundred gifts. If anyone heals a man, let that one give him a reward.

title: What the healer taught his son

plan.english: The father said to his son: 'Look at the stranger. Listen to his words. Do not leave him, and do not grow tired. Good fame comes to the one who sits near. Fire burns the worm; the cord joins the arm.' He heard his father's words.

It dawned. I went to the field and sought the oak's root. I found it and tore it up. I put it into water and heated it. I gave it to the guest, and he drank. Mother Earth gave me the root, and she has rescued him.

title: The horses lay in the field

plan.english: The horses lay in the field and were not standing. The mistress sat beside them, and the fire burned. Then it dawned. She looked at them and said: 'Stand up, and do not be afraid!' Then they stood up and went forth.

The brother was dying, and his sister sat beside him. Grief ate her. She spoke: 'God, do not seize my brother! May he live!' The night went by. At dawn he saw the light, and his sister's heart rejoiced.

Yesterday, son, you went away from your own home. You did not arrive; your father seeks you. The spear wounded you in the field. Your blood goes into the earth, and now your bones lie there. Who shall drive your chariot? And now may your famous name not die. Thrice I cry out for you in the night.
Tears are in my eyes. My son is gone. The wolf did not seize him, the spear did not wound him. Someone has seized him, and I long to see him. And now grief eats my entrails. Who will give him to me?

It has dawned, brother, and you do not come. I look at the field; I did not see you. Your horses arrived, but you did not arrive. And who shall speak to me now? You were the light of my eyes. I remember you.

My husband lies under the oak. No one sits down in his seat. I wear the garment of grief. Now who shall harness the yoke? And now who shall plough my furrow? Come back into my home. And the dead indeed do not listen. May your good fame grow.

The king has died, his fame is great. Now his fame shall be imperishable. And his strength was great. The lords stand and cry out. The chariot is standing, and there is no driver. And now may his famous name be great.

My dog is dead, he was my dear friend. And he followed me along the furrow. And when the wolf arrived, the dear one drove it out. His eyes were bright. Now he lies there below, lie down, dear friend. And who shall stay awake now, in the night?

The strangers arrived, and a blaze devoured the village. And then they carried off the plunder. And now where are my brothers? And now where are my sisters? And now who shall build the village? Perkunos, do you see this?

title: The light returns, we do not

plan.english: The light goes down and comes again. The grain sinks down and grows. When our light has set, we do not come again. We are born, we die. Fame does not die, imperishable fame remains.
The spear wounded me in the head. My blood goes out. I lie down, and it is getting dark. The worms will eat my bones. Tell my sister: he fell by the spear. Do not cry out; my name shall be famous.

It has not rained, the furrow has dried up, the grain does not grow. The wild beasts are thirsty, we are thirsty. We look up, do not leave us. Perkunos, will it not rain? We have grown tired, and our strength is gone.
Dead is my own father. Dead is my sister, my seat has grown cold. Now who shall protect me, who shall lead me? And now who shall clothe me? Then I shall go forth and cry out.

Earth, receive my brother, protect him. And lie down, brother, under the oak. The roots of the oak shall bore through your bones. Last year you grew tall, now you lie below. And now may Perkunos know your name. May your name not vanish.

Man, the swift horses stand at the door. They tremble, and the driver has fallen. Your spear has fallen, your chariot is broken. Who shall yoke them? Who shall drive the chariot? Lie down, man, your name is great.
